row.description: Beginning in the 1st century A.D., Busskirch was a Roman lakeside settlement that served as a stage town on the intersection of the streets to Kempraten respectively Zürich, Winterthur and to Chur respectively on the waterway Walensee–Zürichsee to Rome's alpine route [1]. Today visitors can see the Roman ruins excavated in 1975 underneath Busskirch church [1].
row.card: Underneath Busskirch church lie Roman ruins excavated in 1975, a lakeside Roman site that began in the 1st century A.D. Come and stand above what the Romans left.

row.description: Las Capellanías is a prehistoric funerary complex in Cañaveral de León, Huelva, Spain [1]. Excavation in the area began after road construction workers found a stela in June 2018, and was carried out by staff and students from the universities of Seville, Huelva and Durham [1]. The necropolis was discovered in 2022 [1]. Another stela, found in 2023, has carvings including depictions of a headdress and necklace, usually associated with female burials, but also two swords and male genitalia [1]. It has been described as "gender-bending" and "showing that the social roles depicted by these standardized iconographies were more fluid than previously thought" [1].
row.card: At Las Capellanías in Huelva, a stela found in 2023 is carved with a headdress and necklace, usually associated with female burials, yet also two swords. Described as gender-bending.

row.description: Baalbek was called Heliopolis during the Roman Empire, a latinisation of the Greek Hēlioúpolis used during the Hellenistic period, meaning "Sun City" in reference to the solar cult there [1]. After Alexander the Great's conquest of Persia in the 330s BC, Baalbek formed part of the Diadochi kingdoms of Egypt & Syria [1]. "Baalbek, with its colossal structures, is one of the finest examples of Imperial Roman architecture at its apogee", UNESCO reported in making Baalbek a World Heritage Site in 1984 [1]. Recent cleaning operations at the Temple of Jupiter discovered the deep trench at its edge, whose study pushed back the date of Tell Baalbek's settlement to the PPNB Neolithic [1]. The Tell Baalbek temple complex, fortified as the town's citadel during the Middle Ages, was constructed from local stone, mostly white granite and a rough white marble [1].
row.card: Baalbek's colossal Imperial Roman structures became a World Heritage Site in 1984. At the Temple of Jupiter, a deep trench pushed Tell Baalbek's settlement back to the PPNB Neolithic.

row.description: Trebula or Trebula Balliensis or Trebula Baliensis, was an ancient city of Campania, Italy [1]. The first mention of the name occurs in 303 BCE, when we are told that the Trebulani received the Roman franchise at the same time with the Arpinates [1]. The Liber Coloniarum also mentions Trebula among the municipal towns of Campania [1]. It appears to have received a fresh body of settlers under Augustus, but without attaining the rank of a colony [1]. The site of Trebula, which was erroneously fixed by Cluverius and some local writers to the south of the Vulturnus, appears to be correctly identified by local antiquarians with a place called Treglia or Tregghia, at the foot of the Pizzo San Salvatore, about 10 km north of the Vulturnus and 13 km northeast of Capua [1].
row.card: Look for Trebula Balliensis, an ancient city of Campania, at the foot of the Pizzo San Salvatore: its site appears to be a place called Treglia, about 10 km north of the Vulturnus.

row.description: Lescudjack Hill fort is the name given to the unexcavated Iron Age settlement located in Penzance, Cornwall [1]. It is positioned on the summit of a steep hill in the east of Penzance and consists of a single rampart enclosing an area of 3 acres [1]. The site traditionally was referred to as a castle and Castle Road which runs alongside the site was named after it [1].
row.card: On the summit of a steep hill in east Penzance, a single rampart encloses 3 acres: Lescudjack Hill Fort, an Iron Age settlement traditionally called a castle, which named the road beside it.

row.description: Westbury Camp is a univallate Iron Age hill fort in the Mendip Hills in Somerset [1]. The hill fort is situated in the parish of Rodney Stoke, approximately 1 mile north-east of the village of Draycott and 1.5 miles north-west of Westbury-sub-Mendip [1]. The camp is largely situated on a hill slope [1]. The north east defences have largely been destroyed by small quarries over the years [1]. The narrow top of the hill bank suggests that it may have been surmounted by a dry stone wall [1]. Along part of the east side of the camp there are traces of a berm between the bank and the outer ditch and at the western angle shallow quarry pits occur internally and externally set back from the 'rampart' [1].
row.card: In the Mendip Hills, Westbury Camp is an Iron Age hill fort whose bank, narrow at its top, may once have carried a dry stone wall; small quarries largely destroyed its north east defences.

row.description: The Ġgantija temples are the earliest of the Megalithic Temples of Malta and are older than the pyramids of Egypt [1]. Their makers erected the two Ġgantija temples during the Neolithic, which makes these temples more than 5,500 years old and the world's second-oldest existing manmade religious structures after Göbekli Tepe in present-day Turkey [1]. The temples are elements of a ceremonial site used in a fertility rite [1]. Researchers have found that the numerous figurines and statues found on the site are associated with that cult [1]. The Ġgantija temples stand at the edge of the Xagħra plateau, facing toward the southeast [1]. This megalithic monument encompasses two temples and an incomplete third, of which only the facade was partially built before being abandoned [1]. The southerly one is the larger and older one, dating back to around 3600 BC [1].
row.card: Older than the pyramids of Egypt, the Ġgantija temples stand at the edge of the Xagħra plateau: two Neolithic temples, the southerly one dating to around 3600 BC, and an incomplete third.

row.description: Positioned at the national grid reference 35960865, Hampton Down Stone Circle is located on the southern edge of an open downland ridge at a height of 680 feet above sea level [1]. A photograph from 1908 showed sixteen stones as part of the monument [1]. However, by 1964 twenty-eight stones were found to be part of the circle [1]. In 1964 the stones in the circle were disturbed by agricultural activity [1]. It was then decided that the site would be excavated, a project which was ordered by the Ministry of Public Building and Works and carried out in May 1965 under the directorship of Geoffrey J. Wainwright [1]. The excavation revealed that the location of the stones was not their original prehistoric position [1]. The original location of the circle was identified as existing a few feet to the west [1]. The original circle had either eight or possibly nine sockets for stones and was oval shaped [1].
row.card: The stones of Hampton Down Stone Circle were not in their original position. A May 1965 excavation found the original oval circle a few feet to the west, on a ridge 680 feet above sea level.

row.description: Cunetio was a large walled town in a valley of the River Kennet in modern-day Wiltshire, England [1]. Occupied from the 2nd century AD by Romano-British people, the settlement was abandoned in the early 5th century, the emerging post-Roman period [1]. It lay near what is now the village of Mildenhall, about 1+1⁄2 miles (2.4 km) east of the market town of Marlborough [1]. Artefacts recovered from Cunetio have included kitchenware, personal effects, and two hoards of Roman coinage [1]. In the 1960s, a small coin hoard was found, followed in 1978 by the much larger Cunetio Hoard of over 55,000 coins [1]. The town grew around a mansio that had been built near the crossing of two Roman roads: the east–west road from Speen in Berkshire to Aquae Sulis (Bath), and the south-east to north road from Winchester to Wanborough [1]. As the town grew, it developed a regular grid of streets and stone buildings on its eastern side but retained less regular and substantial structures in the west part [1].
row.card: Cunetio was a large walled town in a valley of the River Kennet in Wiltshire. In 1978 the Cunetio Hoard came to light there: 54,951 coins weighing over 180 kilograms.

row.description: Waithali located in today's northern Rakhine State, Myanmar, was the capital of the Waithali Kingdom from 370 to 818 [1]. Like all of the Arakanese Kingdoms to emerge, the Kingdom of Waithali was based on trade between the East (Pyu city-states, China, the Mons), and the West (India, Bengal, and Persia) [1]. The kingdom flourished off of China-India maritime routes [1]. Waithali was a famed trade port with thousands of ships coming annually at its height [1]. The city was built on the banks of a tidal creek and was enclosed by brick walls [1]. The Waithali site is approximately 70 kilometres north-east of Sittwe, and east of Ram Chaung, a tributary of the Kaladan river [1]. Like its predecessor, Dhanyawadi, the former capital site has fallen into ruin and much of it is now deserted [1]. Only a few temples and traces of the old city wall remain [1].
row.card: On the banks of a tidal creek, brick walls once enclosed Waithali, capital from 370 to 818 of a kingdom that flourished on China-India maritime routes. Only a few temples remain.

row.description: Telmessos or Telmessus, also Telmissus, later Anastasiopolis, then Makri or Macre, was the largest city in Lycia, near the Carian border [1]. The well-protected harbor of Telmessos is separated from the Gulf of Telmessos by an island [1]. The Hittite name was Kuwalapašša, while the Lycian name was Telebehi [1]. In the 13th century BC, the Annals of Hattusili III mentions the city as a part of Lukka and conquered by the Hittites [1]. Telmessos was a flourishing city in the west of Lycia, on the Gulf of Fethiye [1]. It was famed for its school of diviners, consulted among others by the Lydian king Croesus, prior to declaring war against Cyrus [1]. Telmessos was a member of the Delian League in the 5th century BC [1]. It was taken by Alexander the Great in 334 BC, when he came to the town after the siege of Halicarnassus [1].
row.card: An island shelters the harbor of the Ancient City of Telmessos, largest city in Lycia, famed for its school of diviners, consulted among others by the Lydian king Croesus.

row.description: Bhaja Caves are a group of 22 rock-cut caves dating back to the 2nd century BC located off the Mumbai - Pune expressway near the city of Pune [1]. The caves are 400 feet above the village of Bhaja [1]. The most prominent excavation is its chaitya, a good example of the early development of this form from wooden architecture, with a vaulted horseshoe ceiling [1]. Its vihara has a pillared verandah in front and is adorned with unique reliefs [1]. A cistern inscription shows the name of a donor from the 2nd century AD [1]. A notable part of the monument is a group of 14 stupas, five inside and nine outside an irregular excavation [1]. The stupas are relics of resident monks, who died at Bhaja, and display an inscription with the names of three monks, Ampinika, Dhammagiri and Sanghdina [1].
row.card: Bhaja Caves sit 400 feet above the village of Bhaja. Their chaitya has a vaulted horseshoe ceiling, and 14 stupas stand as relics of the monks who died at Bhaja.

row.description: Halikan is an ancient Roman municipium located in present-day Croatia [1]. Founded in the 1st century AD, the municipium had an area of about 3 square kilometres and was a square in ground plan [1]. The wider area was already inhabited earlier by members of the Pannonian tribes, and on the Mura river there was a suitable crossing over that river from one bank to the other [1]. The Romans noticed this and established a military stronghold to monitor the river crossing [1]. Over the time, the settlement developed so much that it became some kind of commercial centre of the surrounding area [1]. The archeological research of Halikan was systematically started by archaeologists of the Međimurje County Museum from Čakovec in 1977 [1]. A pottery furnace and troughs for compacting clay were found among the first finds [1]. The Ara (altar) of the Roman benefactor consul Titus Cesernius Marcilinus, which was dedicated to the supreme god Jupiter, is among the most important discoveries in the territory of the municipium [1].
row.card: The Romans noticed a crossing of the Mura river and built a military stronghold to watch it. Halikan grew into some kind of commercial centre; an altar to Jupiter is among its finds.

row.description: The Wotanstein, also known as 'Wodanstein' or earlier on 'Malstein', is a small megalith or menhir situated close to the village of Maden, Schwalm-Eder-Kreis, Hesse, Germany [1]. The megalith is situated on the south-west corner of the village of Maden, on an elevation between the streams of the Goldbach to the east and Henkelborn to the west [1]. The land on which it stands has an elevation of 177 m [1]. The stone is c. 2.12 m high, 1.2 m wide, and 0.55 m thick [1]. The above-ground volume is thus 1.4 m3 and given quartzite has a density of 2,648 kg/m3, the above-ground stone weighs c. 3.7 metric tons [1]. In 1407 the stone was mentioned in documents as deme langen steyne zu Madin (English: the long stone at Madin (Maden)) [1]. According to oral tradition, during the Seven Years' War (1756–1763) it was excavated because it was rumoured that treasure was buried under it, but remains of human bones were found instead [1].
row.card: Oral tradition says the Wotanstein was dug up in the Seven Years' War for rumoured treasure, but human bones were found instead. In 1407 documents called it the long stone at Madin.

row.description: Juhor is a mountain in central Serbia, near the city of Paraćin [1]. Its highest peak, Veliki Vetren, is at an elevation of 774 metres above sea level [1]. Juhor borders the river Velika Morava to its east and the territory of Levač to its west [1]. Findings from the 3rd century BC in Veliki Vetren include a chest containing some 14 sets of weapons, harness gear, jewelry, and clothing accessories characteristic of knights of Dacian and Scordisci origin [1].
row.card: On Veliki Vetren, the highest peak of Juhor, findings include some 14 sets of weapons, harness gear and jewelry characteristic of knights of Dacian and Scordisci origin.

row.description: Zennor Quoit is a ruined megalithic burial chamber or dolmen, located on a moor about a mile east of the village of Zennor, Cornwall, England [1]. Aside from the 12.5-tonne roof, which collapsed some time between 1770 and 1865, the chamber is in good condition [1]. The quoit measures 12.8 metres in total in diameter [1]. The chamber itself consists of seven upright stones and was originally covered by a cairn [1]. The chamber dates to between 2500 and 1500 BC and is one of eight remaining quoits on the West Penwith moors [1]. Archaeological evidence unearthed on the site has indicated that the chamber was used for the burial of bodies which at some point would be cremated and removed and replaced with others [1]. Excavations at the site have revealed flint and Neolithic style pottery and cremated bones [1]. In 1754 and in 1769, before the roof had fallen, the quoit was analysed by the antiquary Dr. William Borlase, who described and provided detailed drawings of it and published some of his findings in his Antiquities of Cornwall [1].
row.card: On a moor in Cornwall, Zennor Quoit is a ruined dolmen whose chamber of seven upright stones was once covered by a cairn. Digs found flint, Neolithic style pottery and cremated bones.

row.description: Fir Clump Stone Circle was a stone circle in Burderop Wood near Wroughton, Wiltshire, in South West England [1]. The ring was part of a tradition of stone circle construction that spread throughout much of Britain, Ireland, and Brittany during the Late Neolithic and Early Bronze Age, over a period between 3300 and 900 BCE [1]. A double concentric circle consisting of sarsen megaliths, the Fir Clump stone circle was oval-shaped [1]. The outer ring measured 107 metres by 86.5 metres in diameter, and the inner ring 86.5 metres by 73.7 metres [1]. It was one of at least seven stone circles that are known to have been erected in the area south of Swindon in northern Wiltshire [1]. Around the 1860s, the megaliths of Fir Clump stone circle were levelled [1]. Some of the fallen megaliths were rediscovered in 1965 by the archaeologist Richard Reiss, who described and measured the monument [1]. In 1969, these stones were removed during construction of the M4 motorway [1].
row.card: Fir Clump Stone Circle in Burderop Wood was a double oval ring of sarsen megaliths, levelled around the 1860s. Some rediscovered in 1965 were removed in 1969 during construction of the M4.

row.description: The Oppidum de Nages or Oppidum des Castels is on a hilltop overlooking the valley called the Vaunage, above the village of Nages-et-Solorgues, in Gard, between Nîmes et Sommières, in Occitanie [1]. It is one of six iron-age oppida in the Vaunage [1]. The site was excavated and then partially restored, between 1958 and 1974 by the French archaeologist Michel Py [1]. Four stages of construction can be detected [1]. The Volques first occupied the neighbouring Oppidum de Roque de Viou, then about 300 BCE moved into the larger Oppidum des Castel but abandoned it about 50 BCE moving into the Gallo-Roman settlement of Nemausis [1].
row.card: Oppidum des Castels crowns a hilltop above the Vaunage, where four stages of construction can be detected. The Volques moved in about 300 BCE; Michel Py excavated it between 1958 and 1974.

row.description: High Peak is a hill which is partially eroded, resulting in a cliff face, on the English Channel coast to the southwest of Sidmouth, Devon, southern England [1]. Its highest point is about 157 metres above sea-level [1]. It features a partially eroded Iron Age hill fort, with pre-Roman and post Roman pottery found there [1]. On the edge of the cliff there are the remains of significant earthworks, which have been variously shown as having Iron Age, Roman and Dark Age occupation [1]. Geological study, and the lines of the earthworks, suggest that the site once extended several tens of metres into what is now eroded away [1]. General interpretation suggests that it was an Iron Age defensive site which saw re-use in the Dark Age period, perhaps as a coastal trading station [1].
row.card: On the English Channel coast, High Peak rises to about 157 metres above sea-level. Geological study suggests the site once extended several tens of metres into what is now eroded away.

row.description: Dolmen of Carapito I is a megalithic monument located in the civil parish of Carapito, in the municipality of Aguiar da Beira in the Guarda District of Portugal [1]. The dolmen was constructed during the Megalithic period, around 2900 BC [1]. The first explorations of the site were completed by J. Coelho, who collected ceramic fragments [1]. Excavations by Vera Leisner and Leonel Ribeiro were undertaken in 1966 [1]. Located near Guarda, the dolmen is located in a rural landscape, isolated on the western margin of the Ribeira do Carapito [1]. Carapito I is the type of megalithic dolmen characterised by I. Moita as a simple structure with a ten-sided polygonal chamber without a corridor [1].
row.card: Isolated in a rural landscape on the western margin of the Ribeira do Carapito, the Dolmen of Carapito I was excavated in 1966 by Vera Leisner and Leonel Ribeiro.

row.description: The Tarragal Caves are a network of large limestone caves and rockshelters which overlook the Bridgewater Lakes near the towns of Tarragal and Cape Bridgewater [1]. The caves were identified as important Aboriginal camping places early in the historic period, and were excavated in the late 1970s by Harry Lourandos, revealing stratified deposits in the floor of 11,300 years old, along with shell midden deposits and earth ovens over 11,000 years old [1]. One of the caves extends under ground for over 400 m and has a sinkhole opening to the surface so that there is a constant stream of air through the cave and rising up the hole [1]. Pollen analysis of sediments in the cave has assisted in reconstructing the Pleistocene climate and environment of the region and understanding what resources were available to Aborigines [1].
row.card: Above the Bridgewater Lakes, the Tarragal Caves were identified as important Aboriginal camping places. Excavation revealed shell middens and earth ovens over 11,000 years old.

row.description: Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum is an open-air museum in Osmaniye Province, Turkey [1]. The museum is located north of the 638 m-high Karatepe at Kızyusuflu village in Kadirli district of Osmaniye Province [1]. The site contains the remains of an ancient fortress dating back to the 8th century BC [1]. Originally named Azatiwadaya, the walled settlement was founded by Azatiwada, the king of Quwê, a Neo-Hittite kingdom [1]. It was built for defense against invaders from the north [1]. The ruined inner and outer walls of the fortress are 4–6 m high and 2–4 m thick [1]. The fortification stretches over 376 m in the south-north direction and 196 m in the east-west direction [1].
row.card: Karatepe-Aslantaş Open-Air Museum holds the ruined walls of Azatiwadaya, an 8th century BC fortress founded by Azatiwada, a local ruler in Cilicia, to defend against invaders from the north.

row.description: Abbotsbury Castle is an Iron Age hillfort in south west Dorset, England, situated on Wears Hill above the village of Abbotsbury, seven miles west of Dorchester and the famous hill fort at Maiden Castle [1]. It is situated on a high chalk hill overlooking the English Channel [1]. The earthworks cover an area of about 10 acres, of which about 4.5 acres are inside the ramparts [1]. The fort was occupied by the Celtic Durotriges tribe, but when the Romans invaded in AD 43, the second Augustian legion of Vespasian took the fort quickly with little struggle before moving on to Maiden Castle [1]. There is no evidence that the Romans settled at Abbotsbury Castle as they did at some other hill forts [1].
row.card: Abbotsbury Castle, an Iron Age hillfort above the village of Abbotsbury, overlooks the English Channel. Held by the Durotriges, it fell with little struggle to Vespasian's legion in AD 43.

row.description: Qilakitsoq is an abandoned settlement and an important archaeological site in Greenland [1]. It is the location of the discovery of eight mummified corpses from the Thule period [1]. These Inuit mummies offer important insights into the lives of Inuit about 500 years ago [1]. Qilakitsoq is located in Kitaa near the city of Uummannaq on the northern coast of the Nuussuaq peninsula in a sheltered cove of the Karrat Fjord [1]. In the time of the Thule culture, which lasted until about 1800, a settlement of about thirty hunter-gatherers was located here [1]. On October 9, 1972, two hunters discovered a grave containing several mummies while they were out hunting for rock ptarmigans [1]. Radiocarbon dating yielded a probable time of death around 1475 with a margin of error of about ±50 years [1]. A total of 78 articles of clothing were discovered [1].
row.card: Two hunters chasing rock ptarmigans on October 9, 1972 found a grave at Qilakitsoq holding several mummies: Inuit of the Thule period, who probably died around 1475.

row.description: Threestoneburn Stone Circle is an archaeological site, a stone circle near the village of Ilderton and about 5 miles south of Wooler, in Northumberland, England [1]. The circle, of the late Neolithic or early Bronze Age, is situated in a large clearing in the modern afforestation of Threestoneburn Wood, formerly overlooking a spacious valley to the east [1]. It is on a slight promontory near the confluence of Threestone Burn and one of its tributaries [1]. Its dimensions are 36 metres north-west to south-east by 30 metres north-east to south-west [1]. There are 16 stones of local pink granite, set about 5.5 metres apart; a larger gap on the east side is thought to be an original entrance [1]. Four of these are upright, with heights 0.7 to 1.3 metres; the rest are recumbent [1]. A thick layer of peat was found above the ground surface [1]. A flint tool was found, and spreads of charcoal which may be the traces of fire-rituals [1].
row.card: Threestoneburn Stone Circle sets 16 stones of local pink granite in a woodland clearing, four upright. A flint tool was found, and charcoal spreads that may be traces of fire-rituals.

row.description: Al-Rabadha is a settlement in Saudi Arabia located some 200 km to the north-east of Medina on the pilgrim route from Kufa to Mecca, known as Darb Zubaydah [1]. The archaeological excavations directed by King Saud University have shown that Al-Rabadha yields important information for the early phases of Islamic culture [1]. The town is also known as the place where Abu Dharr al-Ghifari spent his last years and died [1]. The excavations at Al-Rabadha give a good insight into urban housing in the Early Islamic Period [1]. The site is dominated by a palace structure, consisting of 13 rooms all with doors opening on a central courtyard [1]. Each room is likely to have served a different purpose, with evidence for ovens, grain storage and a furnace for glass-making found in separate areas [1]. A more typical house from the site is similar in its design, but smaller in area, with divided rooms averaging 3x2m [1]. In contrast with Western Europe, timber is not used in construction, with all houses being made from sun-dried mud brick and having stone foundations [1].
row.card: Al-Rabadha, on the pilgrim route from Kufa to Mecca, is dominated by a palace of 13 rooms opening on a central courtyard, with evidence of ovens, grain storage and a glass-making furnace.

row.description: Duropolis is the name of an archaeological site at Winterborne Kingston in the English county of Dorset, believed to be the remains of the first planned town in Britain [1]. The 32,000 square metres Iron Age settlement is believed to date to around 100 BCE, making it 70 years older than the Roman town of Silchester [1]. The site has been named by archaeologists after the Iron Age Durotriges tribe [1]. Its settlement may have been associated with the abandonment of nearby Maiden Castle in the 1st century BCE [1]. Found in July 2015 by students from Bournemouth University as part of the Durotriges Big Dig project, the remains of 16 Iron Age roundhouses have been excavated while geophysical survey shows a total of at least 150 roundhouses and other features in the area [1]. A number of animal skeletons discovered at the site suggest that the Iron Age Celtic population may have believed in hybrid-animal monster myths akin to those of the Mesopotamians, Ancient Greeks and Egyptians [1].
row.card: Duropolis in Dorset is believed to be Britain's first planned town. Remains of 16 Iron Age roundhouses were dug up, and animal skeletons may hint at a belief in hybrid-animal monster myths.

row.description: Kaminaljuyu is a Pre-Columbian site of the Maya civilization located in Guatemala City [1]. Kaminaljuyu, when first mapped scientifically, comprised some 200 platforms and pyramidal mounds [1]. The site was largely swallowed up by real estate developments [1]. The known parts of Kaminaljuyu lie on a broad plain beneath roughly the western third of modern Guatemala City [1]. The architecture of Middle Preclassic structures consisted of hardened adobe bricks that served, later, as foundations for raised platforms and pyramidal temples [1]. The apogee of Preclassic developments at Kaminaljuyu occurred during what scholars refer to as the "Miraflores" period – once a name for a Late Preclassic ceramic phase, now split into two, the Verbena and Arenal [1]. Enormous thrones and stelae attest to the might and splendor of "Miraflores" Kaminaljuyu [1]. Kaminaljuyu's strategic location also facilitated interactions with central Mexican centers, including Teotihuacan, extending Kaminaljuyu's regional and transregional connections and influence [1].
row.card: Kaminal Juyu Parque Arqueológico, a Maya site in Guatemala City, had some 200 platforms and pyramidal mounds when first mapped scientifically; huge thrones and stelae attest to its might.

row.description: Klimonas is an archaeological site dating to the 9th millennium BC [1]. Discovered in Cyprus at Ayios Tychonas in the Limassol District, Klimonas is the oldest known farming village in the world [1]. The main part of the site is a subterranean circular building approximately ten metres in diameter similar to communal buildings in other nearby sites [1]. Wild boar was hunted and cereals were obtained from the Levant, as well as cats and domesticated dogs [1]. The dogs were used for hunting the boar [1].
row.card: At Ayios Tychonas in the Limassol District of Cyprus lies Klimonas, a village of the 9th millennium BC. Its people hunted wild boar; its cereals and cats came from the Levant.

row.description: Nemea was an ancient sanctuary in the northeastern Peloponnese, today in the regional unit of Corinthia, Greece [1]. Formerly part of the territory of Cleonae in ancient Argolis, its location on neutral ground on the borders of ancient Archaia, Arcadia, Argolis and Corinth was ideal for the creation of a panhellenic religious centre and one of the four prestigious Panhellenic games along with Delphi, Isthmia and Olympia [1]. The Nemean Games were documented from 573 BC, or earlier, at the sanctuary of Zeus at Nemea [1]. The Games were held every two years in July [1]. Greeks gathered for the celebration and a sacred truce was declared to suspend all wars and hostilities for a month in advance so athletes could travel here [1]. The site was excavated in annual campaigns since 1973: many buildings including the great open-air altar, baths, and ancient accommodation for visitors have been unearthed [1].
row.card: At Nemea, an ancient sanctuary of Zeus in the Peloponnese, games were documented from 573 BC, or earlier. Digs since 1973 unearthed a great open-air altar, baths and lodgings for visitors.

row.description: King Ezana's Stele is a 4th century obelisk in the ancient city of Axum, in the Tigray Region of Ethiopia [1]. The monument stands in the middle of the Northern Stelae Park, which contains hundreds of smaller and less decorated stelae [1]. This stele is probably the last one erected and the largest of those that remain unbroken [1]. King Ezana of Axum's Stele stands 21 m tall [1]. It is decorated with a false door at its base and apertures resembling windows on all sides [1]. The stelae are thought to be "markers" for underground burial chambers [1]. The largest grave markers were for royal burial chambers and were decorated with multi-story false windows and false doors; nobility would have smaller, less decorated stelae [1]. King Ezana's Stele is likely to be the last example of this practice, which was abandoned after the Axumites adopted Christianity under King Ezana [1].
row.card: In Axum, King Ezana's Stele stands 21 m tall amid hundreds of smaller stelae, a false door at its base and window-like apertures on all sides. It is likely the last of its kind.

row.description: The Turoe stone is a 1.2 metre tall granite stone decorated in a Celtic style normally located in the village of Bullaun, County Galway, Ireland [1]. It probably dates to about the period 100 BC to AD 100 [1]. The Turoe stone is National Monument of Ireland Number 327 [1]. The top half of the stone is covered with a continuous abstract curvilinear La Tène style design similar to that on the Castlestrange Stone in County Roscommon [1]. The religious or ceremonial purposes of the stone are lost in time [1].
row.card: A curvilinear La Tène style design covers the top half of the Turoe Stone in County Galway, probably from about 100 BC to AD 100. Its religious or ceremonial purposes are lost in time.

row.description: Zar cave is an archaeological site of prehistoric human habitation during the Upper Paleolithic [1]. It is located in the southern part of Zar village, in Kalbajar District, Azerbaijan [1]. During an archaeological campaign in the Kalbajar District from 1981 to 1987, cave paintings of prehistoric humans were discovered [1]. Flint knives, arrowheads and bone combs were also found during the excavations [1]. Traces of dents on discovered boards indicate that they were used for milling wheat [1].
row.card: Zar Cave, an Upper Paleolithic site of prehistoric human habitation, gave up cave paintings, flint knives, arrowheads, bone combs and boards whose dents suggest wheat was milled on them.

row.description: Ahu Akivi is a particular sacred place on the Chilean island of Rapa Nui, looking out towards the Pacific Ocean [1]. Ahu Akivi, aligned in an east–west direction, is located on the flank of the southern slope of Maunga Terevaka at Rapauni and it is surrounded by fairly flat agricultural land [1]. Ahu Akivi is part of the Ahu Akivi-Vai Teka complex which was built up by the Rapa Nui people in two phases [1]. In the first phase, during the 16th century a central rectangular platform was created on a leveled surface [1]. The second phase of construction was elaborately planned and implemented in the early years of the 17th century when the platform was modified, a ramp was created, seven statues of equal size were erected [1]. The seven moai statues are located with absolute astronomical precision [1].
row.card: On Rapa Nui, Ahu Akivi is a sacred place looking out toward the Pacific Ocean, where seven moai of equal size stand on the flank of Maunga Terevaka, built by the Rapa Nui people.

row.description: The Domica cave is a karst cave situated on the south-western border of the Silicka planina Plateau 10 km south-east of Plesivec in the Rožňava District of the Košice Region in southern Slovakia [1]. The cave is well known for its complex structure and high density of speleothems [1]. Jaroslav Böhm directed excavations during the 1930s [1]. Human presence has been documented dating back to the Paleolithic [1]. Post holes from dwelling objects and fireplaces were discovered in several places of the cave [1].
row.card: Domica Cave in Slovakia is well known for its complex structure and dense speleothems. Post holes from dwelling objects and fireplaces were discovered in several places of the cave.

row.description: The Skorba temples are megalithic remains on the northern edge of Żebbiegħ which have provided detailed and informative insight into the earliest periods of Malta's neolithic culture [1]. The site was only excavated in the early 1960s, rather late in comparison to other megalithic sites, some of which had been studied since the early 19th century [1]. The Żebbiegħ area around Skorba appears to have been inhabited very early in the Neolithic period [1]. The remains on the site are a series of megalithic uprights, the lowest course of the temples' foundations, paving slabs with libation holes in the entrance passage, and the torba floor of a three-apse temple [1]. This three-apse shape is typical of the Ġgantija phase [1]. The pottery found on the site is divided into two styles, the Grey Skorba phase distinguished by grey-colored pottery with no motifs, and the Red Skorba phase, which is exactly like the grey Skorba but colored using red ocher [1].
row.card: The Skorba Temples hold paving slabs with libation holes in an entrance passage and the torba floor of a three-apse temple, insight into the earliest periods of Malta's Neolithic culture.

row.description: Shaji-ki-Dheri is the site of an ancient Kanishka stupa about 6 kilometers from Peshawar [1]. French archaeologist Alfred Charles Auguste Foucher had visited Peshawar towards the end of the 19th century, and had noticed two mounds southeast of Peshawar outside the walled city [1]. He tried to relate them to Hiuen Tsang's description of the place [1]. American archaeologist David Brainard Spooner conducted excavations there in 1908-09 for the Archaeological Survey of India leading to the identification of the Kanishka stupa dated to the 2nd century CE, and the discovery of the Kanishka casket [1]. Many statues of the Buddha at Shaji-ki-Dheri feature a halo similar to the haloes seen in the Buddha coins of Kanishka I, suggesting a 2nd century CE date for the creation of the statues, rather than the usual datation to the 3-4th century CE [1].
row.card: Shaji-ki-Dheri, a Kanishka stupa about 6 kilometers from Peshawar, yielded the Kanishka casket in 1908-09. Many Buddha statues there feature haloes like those on Kanishka I's Buddha coins.

row.description: Machu Pitumarka is an archaeological site with ruins of walls in Peru [1]. It is situated in the Cusco Region, Canchis Province, Pitumarca District [1]. Machu Pitumarka lies on a hill northeast of Pitumarka at the southern shore of the river Ch'illkamayu [1].
row.card: On a hill northeast of Pitumarka, at the southern shore of the river Ch'illkamayu, Machu Pitumarka is a site of ruined walls in Canchis Province, in Peru's Cusco Region.

row.description: The Uragh Stone Circle is a small Bronze Age axial stone circle [1]. It is located on the Beara Peninsula, near Gleninchaquin Park, County Kerry, Ireland [1]. Situated between Lough Inchiquin and Lough Cloonee Upper, the site consists of five low megaliths situated next to a large standing stone [1]. Altogether, there are two portal stones, two side stones and the axial (recumbent) stone [1]. The largest standing stone is ten feet (3.0 m) high and the circle is eight feet (2.4 m) in diameter [1]. The centre of the circle has been dug out by treasure seekers [1].
row.card: Between Lough Inchiquin and Lough Cloonee Upper, Uragh Stone Circle has five low megaliths. Its largest standing stone is ten feet high, and treasure seekers dug out its centre.

row.description: La Venta is a pre-Columbian archaeological site of the Olmec civilization located in the present-day Mexican state of Tabasco [1]. La Venta was a civic and ceremonial center [1]. As a ceremonial center, La Venta contains an elaborate series of buried offerings and tombs, as well as monumental sculptures [1]. Complex C, "The Great Pyramid," is the central building in the city layout, is constructed almost entirely out of clay, and is visible from a distance [1]. One of the earliest pyramids known in Mesoamerica, the Great Pyramid is 110 ft (34 m) high and contains an estimated 100,000 cubic meters of earth fill [1]. Seventeen colossal heads have been unearthed in the Olmec area, four of them at La Venta, officially named Monuments 1 through 4 [1]. Frans Blom and Oliver La Farge made the first detailed descriptions of La Venta during their 1925 expedition, sponsored by Tulane University [1]. La Venta was first excavated by Matthew Stirling and Philip Drucker between 1940 and 1943, resulting in several articles by Stirling and in 1952 a two-volume monograph by Drucker [1].
row.card: In Tabasco, the Olmec ceremonial center of La Venta holds buried offerings, tombs and monumental sculptures, among them four colossal heads officially named Monuments 1 through 4.

row.description: Zominthos is a small plateau in the northern foothills of Mount Ida (Psiloritis), on the island of Crete [1]. Zominthos is roughly 7.5 kilometers west of the village of Anogia, on the path from Knossos to Idaion Antron [1]. Zominthos is best known for the large Minoan building discovered there; signs of permanent settlement date back to about 1800 BC [1]. In 1982, the Greek archaeologist Yannis Sakellarakis unveiled a large, two-story Minoan building at an altitude slightly below 1200m [1]. The building's unusual size and careful construction, which incorporates some features pertinent only to palatial architecture, has attracted the interest of archaeologists [1]. Excavations have unearthed only a small part of the building and are still under way [1]. However, they have made clear that the structure has been strongly built and is unusually well-preserved, with some of the remaining walls rising up to 3 meters in height [1].
row.card: In the foothills of Mount Ida on Crete, Zominthos holds a large two-story Minoan building unveiled in 1982, unusually well-preserved, some of its walls still rising up to 3 meters.

row.description: Peinan Site Park (traditional Chinese: 卑南遺址公園; simplified Chinese: 卑南遺址公园; pinyin: Pēinán Yízhǐ Gōngyuán) is an archeological site in Taitung City, Taitung County, Taiwan [1]. The park is the site for the largest and most complete prehistoric settlement ever discovered in Taiwan [1]. The park covers an area of 10,000 square metres and contains more than 1,600 burial sites [1]. Around 20,000 pieces of jade, pottery and stone tools were also found [1].
row.card: Beinan Cultural Park is an archaeological site in Taitung City, home to the largest and most complete prehistoric settlement ever discovered in Taiwan, with more than 1,600 burial sites.

It is also known by its earlier names of the Deadman and Deadman's Point [1]. It hosts the remains of an Iron Age promontory fort, and at its seaward end is "Parson Martin's Cross" – a large granite cross erected in 1896 to encourage those involved in Christian service, and which aids navigation around the headland [1].
row.card: Once known as the Deadman, Dodman Point near Mevagissey is the highest headland on the south Cornwall coast, measuring 374 feet, and it hosts the remains of an Iron Age promontory fort.

row.description: Ariconium was a road station of Roman Britain mentioned in Iter XIII of the Iter Britanniarum of the Antonine Itineraries [1]. It was located at Bury Hill in the parish of Weston under Penyard, about 3 miles east of Ross on Wye, Herefordshire, and about 15 miles southeast of Hereford [1]. The site existed prior to the Roman era, and then came under Roman control [1]. It was abandoned, perhaps shortly after 360, but precisely when and under what circumstances is unknown [1]. Finds have included pre-Roman British coins, including one minted by Cunobelin, and coins from the Roman arrival until 360, after which there are no coins found [1].
row.card: At Bury Hill, Ariconium was a Roman road station, with a pre-Roman coin minted by Cunobelin among its finds. It was abandoned, but precisely when and under what circumstances is unknown.

row.description: Sparsholt Roman Villa was a Roman villa near the village of Sparsholt, Hampshire, England [1]. It was constructed in phases from the 2nd to the 5th century, and then abandoned [1]. It was excavated in 1965–72 [1]. The earliest known house uncovered at Sparsholt was a single-aisled farmhouse probably built in the 2nd century [1]. It may initially have been undivided internally, but by 200 AD it had been replaced by an aisled house with living rooms and a bath suite at one end [1]. In the early 4th century a separate winged-corridor house was constructed at right-angles to the aisled house, and both buildings formed two sides of a rectangular enclosure [1]. Tessellated pavements and mosaics were added to both houses [1]. Trial excavations were conducted in 1890 and 1895 which revealed part of the plan of the villa [1].
row.card: By 200 AD Sparsholt Roman Villa had an aisled house. In the early 4th century a winged-corridor house rose at right angles to it, and both gained tessellated pavements and mosaics.

row.description: Pyramid G1-d is a satellite pyramid within the Khufu pyramid complex on the Giza plateau [1]. The pyramid was discovered in 1992, during work to remove a road, about 25 metres east-southeast of the southeast corner of the Great Pyramid, and about 7 metres west of the subsidiary pyramids G1-b and G1-c [1]. The pyramid's original base length was 21.75 metres, with a height of 13.8 metres [1]. Joseph Dorner established the mean slope to be about 51°45', very similar to that of the Great Pyramid [1]. The substructure consists of an inclined passage of 25–28° which runs north to south [1].
row.card: Work to remove a road in 1992 uncovered Pyramid G1-d, a satellite pyramid of Khufu's complex on the Giza plateau, originally 13.8 metres high, its slope very similar to the Great Pyramid's.

row.description: The Dolmen de Viera or Dolmen de los Hermanos Viera is a dolmen—a type of single-chamber megalithic tomb—located in Antequera, province of Málaga, Andalusia [1]. It is located only 70 metres from the Dolmen of Menga and about 4 kilometres from Tholos de El Romeral [1]. It was discovered in February 1903 by brothers Antonio and Jose Fuentes from Antequera, who also discovered El Romeral [1]. The Dolmen de Viera was built in the Copper Age, 3510-3020 BC approx. It has had the status of a National monument since 1923 [1].
row.card: Only 70 metres from the Dolmen of Menga stands the Dolmen de Viera, a single-chamber tomb found in February 1903 by the brothers José Viera Fuentes and Antonio Viera Fuentes.

row.description: Thuburbo Majus (or Thuburbo Maius) is a large Roman site in northern Tunisia [1]. It is located roughly 60 km southwest of Carthage on a major African thoroughfare [1]. Most of the town was built around 150–200 and restored in the 4th century after the Crisis of the Third Century [1]. It received a Capitolium in 168 [1]. A 1916 excavation found a tetrastyle temple [1]. The building was decorated with statues of Apollo, Venus, Silvanus, Bacchus, the Dioscuri, and a satyr [1]. Remains of the house of Bacchus and Ariadne dating back to the early 5th century were excavated in 1925 [1].
row.card: Roughly 60 km southwest of Carthage, Roman Thuburbo Majus received a Capitolium in 168. A 1916 dig found a tetrastyle temple; the house of Bacchus and Ariadne was excavated in 1925.

row.description: The House of the Greek Epigrams is a Roman residence in the ancient town of Pompeii that was destroyed by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE [1]. It is named after wall paintings with inscriptions from Greek epigrams in a small room next to the peristyle [1]. The home at the time it was destroyed was the result of merging at least two earlier dwellings dating back to the second half of the second century B.C.E. It is estimated this merger occurred around the third quarter of the first century B.C.E. It is thought further alterations took place in the second half of the first century CE as well [1]. The first of the home's rooms were discovered in April 1748 during the very first days of the excavation of Pompeii [1]. More of its rooms were unearthed in late 1875 - 1876 and additional excavations were conducted in 1908 [1]. On November 16 of 1875, a necklace of gold with emeralds and pearls and parts of a silver service as well as an ivory statuette depicting Venus were recovered in the atrium [1].
row.card: Greek epigrams painted on a wall in a small room beside the peristyle gave the House of the Greek Epigrams in Pompeii its name. Its atrium yielded a gold necklace with emeralds and pearls.

row.description: The Flavian Amphitheater, located in Pozzuoli, is the third-largest Roman amphitheater in Italy [1]. Only the Roman Colosseum and the Amphitheatre of Capua are larger [1]. It was likely built by the same architects who previously constructed the Roman Colosseum [1]. The elliptical structure measures 147 by 117 meters, with the arena floor measuring 72.22 by 42.33 meters [1]. The arena can hold up to 50,000 spectators [1]. The interior is mostly intact and one can still see parts of gears, which were used to lift cages up to the arena floor [1]. In 305, the arena was the setting for the persecutions of the patron saint of Pozzuoli, Saint Proculus, and the patron saint of Naples, Saint Januarius [1].
row.card: The interior of the Flavian Amphitheatre at Pozzuoli is mostly intact, and one can still see parts of the gears that were used to lift cages up to the arena floor.

row.description: Bhamala Stupa is a ruined Buddhist stupa near Haripur, Pakistan, that dates to the 2nd century CE [1]. It is located on the banks of the Haro River, near Khanpur Dam [1]. Bhamala stupa is part of the larger Bhamala Buddhist Complex [1]. The site is known for its 1,700-year-old statue of the Buddha attaining enlightenment—considered to be the oldest such statue in the world [1]. Dating to the 2nd–5th century CE, the site was first excavated by John Marshall in 1929, and work continued until the early 1930s; excavations resumed in 2017 [1]. According to current understanding, the shape of the main stupa is cruciform, and it is the largest surviving example of this shape in the Taxila and Gandhara regions [1]. There are about nineteen small, votive stupas in the courtyard surrounding the main one [1].
row.card: On the banks of the Haro River, the ruined Bhamala Stupa dates to the 2nd century CE. Step among its ruins and read for yourself what the centuries have left behind.

row.description: The Chuping Archaeological Site (traditional Chinese: 曲冰考古遺址; simplified Chinese: 曲冰考古遗址; pinyin: Qūbīng Kǎogǔ Yízhǐ) is an archaeological site in Ren'ai Township, Nantou County, Taiwan [1]. It houses relics of the first prehistoric mountain settlements in Taiwan [1]. The site was discovered in 1980 in the upper area of Zhuoshui River valley [1]. Three excavations were performed there between 1981 and 1987 [1]. The site was later covered again as a protective measure, with the intention of eventually transforming it into an educational exhibit [1]. The site is located at an altitude of 750 metres [1].
row.card: Covered over again to protect it, the Chuping Archaeological Site in Ren'ai Township, Nantou County, holds relics of the first prehistoric mountain settlements in Taiwan.

row.description: The Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania is a funerary monument located on the road between Cherchell and Algiers, in Tipaza Province, Algeria [1]. The Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania is a common type of ancient mausoleums found in Algeria built on a hill some 250 metres above sea level [1]. The monument is entirely built from stone, while its main structure is in a circular form with a square base topped by a cone or a pyramid [1]. The height of the monument was originally about 40 metres or 130’ in height [1]. The base of the monument was decorated with 60 Ionic columns whose capitals were removed, possibly stolen [1]. The mausoleum was built in 3 BC by the King of Mauretania, Juba II and his wife Cleopatra Selene II [1].
row.card: Between Cherchell and Algiers, the Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania once stood about 40 metres high, its base decorated with 60 Ionic columns. Its date and real function are uncertain.

row.description: The earliest history of the creation of Longmen Grottoes is traced to the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei dynasty when he shifted his capital to Luoyang from Datong; Luoyang's symbolic value is borne by the fact that it served as the historic capital for 13 dynasties [1]. The site was subjected to significant vandalism after the fall of the Qing dynasty [1]. The Longmen Grottoes represent a critical period in the evolution of Chinese Buddhist sculpture [1]. Scholarly analysis of the site's Buddhist imagery, particularly from the Northern Dynasties to the Tang dynasty, has revealed a gradual synthesis of imported Central Asian artistic conventions with indigenous Chinese aesthetic traditions [1]. Guyangdong, or Guyang Cave, or Old Sun Cave, is recorded as the oldest Longmen cave with carvings in the Northern Wei style [1]. Also found here are 600 inscriptions in fine calligraphy of writings in the Northern Wei style [1].
row.card: The earliest history of the Longmen Grottoes is traced to the reign of Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei. Guyang Cave, the Old Sun Cave, is recorded as the oldest with Northern Wei carvings.

row.description: Deir el-Medina, or Dayr al-Madīnah, is an ancient Egyptian workmen's village which was home to the artisans who worked on the tombs in the Valley of the Kings during the 18th to 20th Dynasties of the New Kingdom of Egypt (ca. 1550–1080 BC) [1]. The site is located on the west bank of the Nile, across the river from modern-day Luxor [1]. The village is laid out in a small natural amphitheatre, within easy walking distance of the Valley of the Kings to the north, funerary temples to the east and south-east [1]. A French team directed by Bernard Bruyère excavated the entire site, including village, dump and cemetery, between 1922 and 1951 [1]. The first datable remains of the village belong to the reign of Thutmose I (c. 1506–1493 BC) with its final shape being formed during the Ramesside Period [1]. In about the 25th year of the reign of Ramesses III (c. 1170 BC) the tomb laborers were so exasperated by delays in supplies that they threw down their tools and walked off the job in what may have been the first sit-down strike action in recorded history [1].
row.card: Across the Nile from Luxor, artisans of Deir el-Medina worked on the tombs in the Valley of the Kings. Exasperated by delays in supplies, they threw down their tools and walked off.

row.description: Stane Street is the modern name of the 91 km-long Roman road in southern England that linked Londinium (London) to Noviomagus Reginorum (Chichester) [1]. The exact date of construction is uncertain; however, on the basis of archaeological artefacts discovered along the route, it was in use by 70 AD and may have been built in the first decade of the Roman occupation of Britain (as early as 43–53 AD) [1]. Stane Street shows clearly the engineering principles that the Romans used when building roads [1]. Stane is an old spelling of "stone" which was commonly used to differentiate paved Roman roads from muddy native trackways [1]. For much of its length, Stane Street consisted of a central agger, with parallel ditches either side [1]. Mansiones have been identified on Stane Street at Alfoldean and Hardham [1]. The mansio at Hardham is thought to have become disused by the end of the second century AD and the road is absent from the third-century Antonine Itinerary [1]. Nevertheless, Stane Street continued to be an important trade route until at least the early fourth century [1].
row.card: Stane Street, a Roman road of 91 km from London to Chichester, was in use by 70 AD. For much of its length it had a central agger with parallel ditches either side.

row.description: Welbeck Hill is the site of Roman and early Saxon pottery finds, and an Anglo-Saxon cemetery, located around 1.75 miles from Laceby, and around 3 miles from Riby, in North East Lincolnshire [1]. Excavations on the southern slope of Welbeck Hill led to finds of a Roman 'grey ware dish and lug handle, also heavy well-fired shards and a cooking pot with a flat topped rim' [1]. Excavations of the Anglo-Saxon cemetery were begun by G. Taylor in 1962 after ploughing disturbed remains [1]. Three burial areas, dating from around the mid-5th and 6th centuries, have since been identified; north/south along the hill crest, east/west on the hill's western slope and a deposit of cremations on the eastern slope [1]. From 1962 to July 1976, 76 graves and 5 cremations were recorded [1].
row.card: Ploughing disturbed remains on Welbeck Hill; excavations began in 1962 at an Anglo-Saxon cemetery: burials along the hill crest, cremations on the eastern slope, 76 graves by July 1976.

row.description: Vertillum is a Gallo-Roman site in the modern commune of Vertault in the Côte-d'Or department of eastern France [1]. Vertillum was classified as a Historical Monument in 1875 [1]. It includes many buried structures, remains of ramparts, thermal baths and a temple [1]. A Gallic oppidum covering about 25 hectares originally occupied the site, surrounded by a stone wall and ditch [1]. Later it evolved into a Gallo-Roman settlement with the typical features of such cities: residential areas, a forum, baths, temple and administrative center [1]. The Roman town would have had between 3,000 and 5,000 inhabitants [1]. Vertillum was a center for working copper-based alloys [1]. Unfinished objects and waste material show that the smiths used foundry techniques to work sheet iron and to bronze the iron objects [1].
row.card: Vertillum began as a Gallic oppidum and grew into a Gallo-Roman town of perhaps 3,000 to 5,000 people, a center for working copper-based alloys, with remains of ramparts, baths and a temple.

row.description: The Huaca Huantinamarca is an archaeological site of the Ichma culture located in San Miguel District, in Lima, Peru [1]. The Huaca Huantinamarca Research, Conservation and Restoration Project identified at least two fundamental phases in its construction [1]. During the first phase, walls of various sizes were built, with predominance of walls 40 and 80 cm thick, using a technique known as formwork [1]. In the second phase, walls with blocks of regular dimensions, a section of which displays a trapezoidal form, which are more structurally stable, were used [1]. Huantinamarca was part of the Maranga complex, and served as the main seat of a community, integrated into the productive and ritual chain linked to the collection, transformation, and consumption of corn chicha used in celebrations and rituals associated with the agricultural calendar [1]. Fragmented ceramic material, vessels and funerary offerings found during excavations are related to the late Ichma period, and some have Chancay and Chimu influence [1].
row.card: In Lima, Huaca Huantinamarca, an Ichma culture site built in at least two phases, was the main seat of a community linked to the collection, transformation and consumption of corn chicha.

row.description: Kotosh is an archaeological site near the town of Huánuco, Peru, consisting of a series of buildings comprising six periods of continuous occupation [1]. The Kotosh Period culture stratum was situated directly beneath the Chavin culture stratum [1]. Some Kotosh elements show links with the Chavin culture [1]. Kotosh Black Polished Incised pottery is similar to Classical Chavin pottery [1]. The Wairajirca period continued from the late eighteenth to late twelfth century cal BC (1750-1150 BC) [1]. The Kotosh Period strongly maintained the traditions of the preceding Wairajirca Period, including the ceramic tradition [1]. The image of crossed arms is characteristic for the Kotosh temple iconography [1].
row.card: Near Huánuco, Kotosh holds buildings from six periods of occupation, its Kotosh Period layer lying directly beneath the Chavin one. In its temple art, a signature image: crossed arms.

row.description: Grange stone circle is a stone circle in County Limerick, Ireland [1]. It is located 300m west of Lough Gur, 4 km north of Bruff [1]. The Limerick-Kilmallock road is nearby [1]. It is estimated to be 4,000-years-old, dating from the Bronze Age [1]. The largest stone is Rannach Chruim Duibh and is over 4m high and weighs 40 tonnes [1]. The entrance of the circle is aligned with the rising sun at the summer solstice [1]. A short distance to the north-north east of the main stone circle, is a second smaller circle, also constructed of large stones [1]. To the north of this is a large leaning standing stone [1].
row.card: Near Lough Gur, the Grange Stone Circle raises its largest stone, Rannach Chruim Duibh, over 4m high and weighing 40 tonnes. A second, smaller circle and a large leaning stone lie nearby.

row.description: Chanhudaro is one of the most important sites of Indus civilization [1]. Chanhu-Daro was investigated in 1931 by the Indian archaeologist N. G. Majumdar [1]. Evidence of shell working was found at Chanhudaro and bangles and ladles were made at this site [1]. Copper knives, spears, razors, tools, axes, vessels and dishes were found [1]. Indus Seals are also found at Chanhudaro and Chanhudaro is considered one of the centres where seals were manufactured [1].
row.card: Investigated in 1931 by N. G. Majumdar, Chanhudaro shows evidence of shell working. Bangles and ladles were made here, and it is considered one of the centres where seals were manufactured.

row.description: The Amphitheatre of El Jem is an oval amphitheatre in the modern-day city of El Djem, Tunisia, formerly Thysdrus in the Roman province of Africa [1]. The amphitheatre was built around 238 AD in Thysdrus, located in the Roman province of Africa Proconsularis in present-day El Djem [1]. It is one of the best preserved Roman stone ruins in the world, and is unique in Africa [1]. Like other amphitheatres in the Roman Empire, it was built for spectator events, and it is one of the biggest amphitheatres in the world [1]. The estimated capacity is 35,000, and the major and minor axes respectively measure 148 metres and 122 metres [1]. The amphitheatre is built of stone blocks, located on flat ground, and is exceptionally well conserved [1]. The amphitheatre of El Jem is the third amphitheatre built in the same place [1].
row.card: On flat ground stands El Jem Amphitheatre, an oval whose axes measure 148 metres and 122 metres. Exceptionally well conserved, it is one of the biggest amphitheatres in the world.

row.description: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the largest of the Egyptian pyramids and the most famous landmark of the Giza pyramid complex in Giza, Egypt [1]. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only wonder that has remained largely intact [1]. The Great Pyramid served as the tomb of Egyptian Pharaoh Khufu, who ruled during the Fourth Dynasty of the Old Kingdom [1]. It was built c. 2600 BC over a period of about 26 years [1]. The Great Pyramid was built by quarrying an estimated 2.3 million large blocks, weighing 6 million tonnes in total [1]. The funerary complex around the pyramid consisted of two mortuary temples connected by a causeway; tombs for the immediate family and court of Khufu, including three smaller pyramids for Khufu's wives; an even smaller "satellite pyramid"; and five buried solar barques [1].
row.card: Tomb of Khufu, the Great Pyramid of Giza rose circa 2600 BC from an estimated 2.3 million quarried blocks. East of it, three boat-shaped pits are large enough to have held complete boats.

row.description: Fleam Dyke is a linear earthwork between Fulbourn and Balsham in Cambridgeshire, initiated some time between AD 330 and AD 510 [1]. The dyke is located near Cambridge, between Fulbourn and Balsham [1]. It forms a barrier across an open chalkland ridge, bounded near Fulbourn by marshy fenland and near Balsham by 90-metre-high formerly wooded hills [1]. It is three miles long and seven metres high from ditch to bank [1]. In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries Anglo-Saxon weapons and burials were found [1]. An excavation in 1991, on occasion of widening the A11 road, established by radiocarbon dating that it had been built in several phases, the first between AD 330 and 510, and the last between AD 450 and 620 [1].
row.card: Fleam Dyke, a linear earthwork between Fulbourn and Balsham, gave up Anglo-Saxon weapons and burials. In 1991, radiocarbon dating showed it was built in several phases.

row.description: The Temple of Hercules Gaditanus, Temple of Melqart or Temple of Hercules-Melqart was a place of worship in Antiquity in the southern outskirts of Gadir-Gades (current-day Cádiz), perhaps dating as early as the 8th century BC [1]. Operating under Tyrian, Carthaginian and Roman rule, it once was one of the most important sanctuaries in the Western World [1]. It was paid respect by the likes of Hannibal, Scipio Africanus and Caesar [1]. It was initially dedicated to the Phoenician god Melqart and then to Hercules [1]. The sanctuary was likely a complex of buildings where the main structure could be accessed through a gateway flanked by two large columns [1].
row.card: On the southern outskirts of Gadir-Gades, perhaps as early as the 8th century BC, the Temple of Hercules Gaditanus was dedicated to Melqart, then Hercules. Hannibal and Caesar paid respect.

row.description: The Castro of Vieito is an archaeological site of the Castro culture of northwestern Iberian Peninsula, situated on the right margin of the Lima River estuary, in the civil parish of Perre, municipality of Viana do Castelo [1]. Lasting for a century, the settlement corresponded to the initial Romanization of the northwest corner of the Iberian Peninsula (from the late 1st century BCE to the first half of the 1st century AD, or as late as the year 70) [1]. The settlement is considered modest, with characteristics common for the larger settlements: such as a wall with monumental entrance-ways; the organization of the family living spaces and barrios; paved floors; a circular great house with bunk seating along the wall; and a home with rectangular courtyard, in addition to Roman coins in silver and bronze, amphorae, and rings [1].
row.card: On the Lima River estuary, the Castro of Vieito lasted a century: a settlement considered modest, with a wall with monumental entrance-ways, a circular great house and Roman coins.

row.description: Listoghil (Irish: Lios an tSeagail) is the large central monument in the Carrowmore group of prehistoric tombs in County Sligo, Ireland [1]. The Carrowmore group consists of about 35 monuments surrounding Listoghil [1]. It was numbered as Carrowmore 51 by George Petrie in 1837 and this designation is still used [1]. Listoghil stands 59 meters above sea level at the geographic centre of the Cúil Iorra Peninsula, c. 3 km from Sligo town [1]. Listoghil is larger than its satellites, being about 34 meters in diameter; the satellites average about 15 meters [1]. By the end of the 19th century the tomb had been investigated by antiquarians of the period who recorded finding 'bones of horses', charred wood and a worked flint javelin head [1]. In the late 1990s, Goran Burenhult, a Swedish archaeologist, partly excavated Listoghil [1]. The chamber at the heart of the mound is a dolmen-like structure, with 6 orthostats [1].
row.card: Listoghil spans about 34 meters at the heart of the Carrowmore tombs, ringed by about 35 monuments. Antiquarians recorded finding 'bones of horses', charred wood and a flint javelin head.

row.description: The Pipers are a pair of standing stones near The Merry Maidens stone circle located 2 miles to the south of the village of St Buryan, in Cornwall, United Kingdom [1]. The Pipers are on a northeast to southwest alignment which points almost directly at The Merry Maidens [1]. The two stones stand in separate fields about 90 metres apart [1]. The southwest stone is the taller of the two, measuring 4.7 metres high—there are two longitudinal cracks down the northwest side, and one down the southeast side [1]. The northeast stone is 4.2 metres high and is of rectangular section—the stone leans to the northwest [1]. The stones were first recorded by William Borlase in 1754 [1]. His descendant William Copeland Borlase excavated the stones in 1871 with no result [1].
row.card: In Cornwall, The Pipers, two standing stones in separate fields about 90 metres apart, point almost directly at The Merry Maidens. An excavation in 1871 brought no result.

row.description: Chichen Itza was a major focal point in the Northern Maya Lowlands from the Late Classic (c. 600–900 AD) through the Terminal Classic (c. 800–900 AD) and into the early portion of the Postclassic period (c. 900–1200 AD) [1]. The Maya name "Chichén Itzá" means "At the mouth of the well of the Itzá" [1]. Chichen Itza is located in the eastern portion of the Mexican state of Yucatán [1]. Between 900 and 1050 AD Chichen Itza expanded to become a powerful regional capital controlling north and central Yucatán [1]. The earliest hieroglyphic date discovered at Chichen Itza is equivalent to 832 AD, while the last known date was recorded in the Osario temple in 998 [1]. Archeological data now indicates that Chichen Itza declined as a regional center by 1100 [1]. Chichen Itza was one of the largest Maya cities, with the relatively densely clustered architecture of the site core covering an area of at least 5 square kilometers [1]. Dominating the North Platform of Chichen Itza is the Temple of Kukulcán [1].
row.card: Chichén Itzá, in eastern Yucatán, was one of the largest Maya cities, its name meaning "At the mouth of the well of the Itzá". The Temple of Kukulcán dominates its North Platform.

row.description: The Castro of Monte Castelo is a Calcolithic fortified settlement, situated in the civil parish of Custóias, Leça do Balio e Guifões, in the municipality of Matosinhos in the northern Portuguese district of Porto [1]. In 1878, there were archaeological excavations under the direction of Francisco Martins Sarmento [1]. The site is situated on the periphery of Guifões, on the eastern flank of a hilltop overlooking the town, surrounded by pine forests, overlooking the Leça River [1]. The fortified settlement is defended by three lines of walls [1]. On the western flank, the area has been excavated, resulting in the unearthing of family homes of circular and rectangular plans [1].
row.card: Three lines of walls defend the Castro of Monte Castelo, a fortified settlement among pine forests above the Leça River, where excavation unearthed homes of circular and rectangular plans.

row.description: The Rock carvings of Boglösa in the province of Uppland in central Sweden are located to the southeast of Enköping [1]. The three petroglyphs (Swedish: Hällristningar) form part of a complex of rock art [1]. They derive from the Swedish Bronze Age (c.1500-500 BC) and the Iron Age [1]. Among the Hällristningar, which depict ships, the 4.13 m long and 0.6 m high Brandskogsskeppet stands out [1]. The unparalleled, naturalistically depicted, compact hull is decorated at the ends with the heads of moose [1]. The crew consists of six rowers [1]. This image is dated to the beginning of the Iron Age [1].
row.card: Southeast of Enköping, the Rock Carvings of Boglösa depict ships. One, the 4.13 m long Brandskogsskeppet, has a compact hull with moose heads at the ends and a crew of six rowers.

row.description: Fin Cop is a hill and an associated Iron Age hill fort in Monsal Dale, close to Ashford in the Water in Derbyshire, England [1]. The fort shows evidence of hurried construction, indicating a defensive response to a real threat, rather than the more usual assumption that such forts were a display of status and prestige [1]. In 2011 excavations unearthed a mass burial containing only women and children, probably massacred after the fort was attacked, the first such segregated burial in Iron Age Britain [1]. Some animal bones were also found, suggesting the inhabitants kept livestock [1]. The remains were relatively well preserved due to the limestone geology of the hill [1]. Carbon dating of the site suggests it was constructed between 440BC and 390BC [1].
row.card: Fin Cop's Iron Age hill fort in Monsal Dale shows signs of hurried building. Excavation unearthed a mass burial of only women and children, probably massacred after the fort was attacked.

row.description: The Cave of Altxerri is located in the municipality of Aya in the Basque Country [1]. The original grotto preserves rock paintings and engravings which have been dated from the end of the Upper Magdalenian period, within the Upper Paleolithic; the pictures situated in an upper gallery, known as Altxerri B, have been dated in a 2013 study as the oldest stone paintings in Europe, with an estimated age of 39,000 years [1]. Its artistic style forms part of the so-called Franco-Cantabrian School [1]. Altxerri houses one of the largest sets of rock engravings of the area [1]. It contains around one hundred and twenty engravings of which ninety-two are of animals [1]. The bison is the best-represented animal, with a total of fifty-three engravings [1]. Other animals present in the cave are the reindeer, with six engravings, four deer and goats, three horses and aurochs, two saiga antelope, a wolverine, a fox, a hare and a bird [1]. It was declared a World Heritage Site in 2008 as part of the group known as the Cave of Altamira and Paleolithic Cave Art of Northern Spain [1].
row.card: In the Cave of Altxerri, bison, reindeer, a wolverine and a fox are engraved in the rock, while paintings in an upper gallery were estimated in a 2013 study at 39,000 years old.

row.description: Trogir is a historic town and harbour on the Adriatic coast in Split-Dalmatia County, Croatia [1]. The historic part of the city is situated on a small island between the Croatian mainland and the island of Čiovo [1]. It lies 27 kilometres west of the city of Split [1]. Since 1997, the historic centre of Trogir has been included in the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites for its Venetian architecture [1]. In the 3rd century BC, Tragurion was founded as a colony by Ancient Greek colonists on the Illyrian coast from the island of Vis, and it developed into a major port until the Roman period [1]. Trogir has 2300 years of continuous urban tradition [1].
row.card: Trogir's historic heart sits on a small island between the Croatian mainland and Čiovo, 27 kilometres west of Split. Since 1997, UNESCO has listed it as a World Heritage Site.

row.description: Eketorp is an Iron Age fort, located in southeastern Öland, Sweden, and extensively reconstructed and enlarged in the Middle Ages [1]. Eketorp is the only one of the 19 known prehistoric fortifications on Öland that has been completely excavated, yielding a total of over 24,000 individual artifacts [1]. The indigenous peoples of the Iron Age constructed the original fortification about 400 AD [1]. The ringfort in that era is thought to have been a gathering place for religious ceremonies and also a place of refuge for the local agricultural community when an outside enemy appeared [1]. The original diameter of this circular stone fortification was about 57 metres [1]. In the next century the stone was moved outward to construct a new circular structure of about 80 metres in diameter [1]. At this juncture there were known to be about fifty individual cells or small structures within the fort as a whole [1].
row.card: On Öland, Eketorp began as a circular stone fort about 57 metres across, thought to be a place of religious ceremonies and refuge; its full excavation yielded over 24,000 artifacts.

row.description: Phylaki is a modern village and the archaeological site of an ancient Minoan cemetery on Crete [1]. The site, discovered in 1981, is a Late Minoan IIIA tholos tomb [1]. At least 9 burials were made here [1]. Artefacts found included a gold necklace which contained 28 rosettes of gold, fifteen seal stones, amulets, bronze weapons and bronze utensils [1].
row.card: At Phylaki on Crete, a Late Minoan IIIA tholos tomb discovered in 1981 held at least 9 burials, a gold necklace, seal stones, amulets, and bronze weapons and utensils.

row.description: Quelfénnec is an archaeological site in the French commune of Plussulien, in the Côtes-d'Armor department of Brittany [1]. The site is a dolerite quarry which was exploited in the Neolithic period for the production of polished stone tools [1]. Quelfennec's axes have been found throughout western France, but also in North-West Europe, the British Isles, and Belgium [1].
row.card: In the Côtes-d'Armor department of Brittany, Quelfénnec was a dolerite quarry worked in the Neolithic for polished stone tools, and its axes have been found throughout western France.

row.description: Koumasa is a Minoan archaeological site in southern Crete, best known for its large prepalatial cemetery [1]. It is located between the villages of Loukia and Koumasa, at the southern edge of the Mesara Plain and near the foothills of the Asterousia Mountains [1]. The site was first excavated by Stephanos Xanthoudides between 1904 and 1906 [1]. Koumasa includes both a Prepalatial cemetery and an associated settlement extending across the saddle of the Korakies hill [1]. The site is also notable for its marble folded-arm figurines, which combine Cycladic features with local Minoan styles [1]. The burial architecture at Koumasa is dominated by large circular tholos tombs constructed during the Prepalatial Minoan period [1]. These tombs are built from locally sourced limestone, employing dry-stone construction techniques without the use of mortar [1]. Outside Tholos B, a secondary burial deposit yielded an assemblage of 140 multicolored beads, seven stone seals, gold foil bands, a small rock crystal phiale, obsidian blades, and bronze tools [1].
row.card: At Koumasa in southern Crete, Minoan tholos tombs were built of limestone without mortar. Outside one, a burial deposit held 140 multicolored beads and bands of gold foil.

row.description: Koonalda Cave is a cave in the Australian state of South Australia, on the Nullarbor Plain [1]. It is located within the Nullarbor Wilderness Protection Area, 99 kilometres west of the Nullarbor roadhouse and 97 kilometres north east from Eucla, Western Australia [1]. Thousands of square metres in the cave are covered in parallel finger-marked geometric lines and patterns, Aboriginal Australian artwork which has been dated as 20,000 years old [1]. The cave was abandoned 19,000 years ago [1]. Analysis of finger markings and archaeological deposits showed that Aboriginal people used the cave 22,000 years ago [1]. The cave was explored by an expedition led by Captain J. M. Thompson in 1935 [1]. In the 1960s, the cave was excavated by Alexandor Gallus, who found that Aboriginal people had mined flint there [1].
row.card: On the Nullarbor Plain, Koonalda Cave bears finger-marked geometric lines and patterns, Aboriginal Australian artwork dated as 20,000 years old. Aboriginal people also mined flint there.

row.description: Sexi, also known as Ex, was a Phoenician colony at the present-day site of Almuñécar on southeastern Spain's Mediterranean coast [1]. The Roman name for the place was Sexi Firmum Iulium [1]. Alternative transcriptions of the Phoenician name of the city in Latin include Secks, Seks, Sex, Eks, Seksi and Sexsi [1]. The ancient Phoenician settlement, whose earliest phases are unclear, was located southwest of the Solorius Mons [1]. From the 3rd-2nd centuries BC it issued a sizable corpus of coinage, with many coins depicting the Phoenico-Punic god Melqart on the obverse and one or two fish on the reverse, possibly alluding to the abundance of the sea and also a principal product of the area [1].
row.card: On the Mediterranean coast at Almuñécar lay Sexi, a Phoenician colony. Many of its coins of the 3rd-2nd centuries BC show the god Melqart on one face and one or two fish on the other.

row.description: The Stoa of Eumenes was constructed south of the Asklepieion staircase and the peripatos, on an artificial terrace of 9m x 13ms [1]. To retain the pathway to the north an arched retaining wall was constructed along the northern edge of the site [1]. Along this wall, the remains of which now dominate the site, the arcade was built [1]. A substantial part of its northern wall, which is made from breccia and limestone and faced with Hymettian and Pentelic marble, is still preserved [1].
row.card: The Stoa of Eumenes rose south of the Asklepieion staircase, its arcade built along an arched wall that retained the pathway to the north. A substantial part of the northern wall survives.
