row.description: Delos or Dilos, is a small Greek island near Mykonos, close to the centre of the Cyclades archipelago [1]. Though only 3.43 km2 in area, it is one of the most important mythological, historical, and archaeological sites in Greece [1]. Between 900 BC and 100 AD, Delos was a major cult centre, where the gods Dionysus and Leto, mother of the twin deities Apollo and Artemis, were revered [1]. In 167 or 166 BC, after the Roman victory in the Third Macedonian War, the Roman Republic ceded Delos to the Athenians [1]. The Roman destruction of Corinth in 146 BC allowed Delos to at least partially assume Corinth's role as the premier trading centre of Greece, but Delos' commercial prosperity, construction activity, and population waned significantly after the island was assaulted by the forces of Mithridates VI of Pontus in 88 and 69 BC [1]. Before the end of the first century BC, trade routes had changed; Delos was replaced by Puteoli as the chief focus of Italian trade with the east, and as a cult centre it entered a sharp decline [1].
row.card: The Roman Republic ceded Delos to the Athenians in 167 or 166 BC. After Rome destroyed Corinth in 146 BC, Delos at least partially assumed its role as premier trading centre of Greece.

row.description: The Panóias Sanctuary, also called "Fragas de Panóias", is located in Vale de Nogueiras, in the municipality of Vila Real, Portugal [1]. Its construction dates back to the end of the 2nd century - early 3rd century AD [1]. The sanctuary is an enclosure with three large rocks, where several cavities of various sizes were opened and access stairs were also built [1]. On the rock located at the entrance of the enclosure, several inscriptions were engraved - three in Latin and one in Greek, describing the ritual celebrated [1].
row.card: Santuário Rupestre de Panóias is an enclosure of three large rocks with cavities opened in them and stairs built. On the entrance rock, Latin and Greek inscriptions describe the ritual.

row.description: La Almoloya is an archaeological site in Murcia, the southeast corner of the Iberian Peninsula in modern-day Spain [1]. It is a principal site of study for the Bronze Age Argaric culture that flourished from about 2200 BC to 1500 BC and controlled territory in Iberia that is equivalent in size to modern Belgium [1]. The site includes the find of what is described as an "especially rich" grave 38, which was excavated beginning in 2014 [1]. It contains the skeletal remains of a woman and a man [1]. The vast majority of the grave goods are associated with the woman; it contains numerous silver grave goods, including a diadem [1]. The couple is buried beneath the floor of a large building [1]. Radiocarbon dating suggests the burial took place at approximately 1700 BC [1]. According to Lull et al., the building above the grave may be one of the earliest Bronze Age palaces identified in Western Europe [1].
row.card: At La Almoloya, a woman and a man lie beneath the floor of a large building, their grave holding numerous silver goods including a diadem. Radiocarbon dating suggests approximately 1700 BC.

row.description: The Kriemhildenstuhl lies left of the small river of the Isenach northwest of Bad Dürkheim at a height of 250 metres above sea level on the southeastern hillside of the 300-metre-high Kästenberg [1]. Archaeological excavations were carried out in 1884, 1893/94, 1916/17, 1934/35 and 1937–1939 [1]. Quarrying was undertaken using several working parties, so-called Arbeitsköpfe [1]. Individual Arbeitsköpfe were 25 metres above the next level below [1].

row.description: Woodbury Hill is a hill near Bere Regis in Dorset, England [1]. It is the site of an Iron Age hillfort, and the location of an annual fair from medieval times until the mid 20th century [1]. The hill overlooks the Winterbourne Valley to the north and the Piddle Valley to the south; immediately to the west is Bere Stream [1]. The irregularly-shaped hillfort has an area of about 5 hectares (12 acres) [1]. It is about 272 metres (892 ft) west to east and 410 metres (1,350 ft) north to south, and is enclosed by a single rampart of width 6 to 12 metres (20 to 39 ft); outside this is a ditch of width 9 metres (30 ft) and a counterscarp [1]. The ground outside the defences falls steeply to the east, south and south-west [1]. To the north, where there is a gently sloping strip of land leading to a northern ridge, a second rampart about 60 metres (200 ft) north of the main rampart provides additional defence [1]. There is an original entrance on the south-west, through which a track leads into the fort, and an original entrance on the north-east; other breaks in the defences are more recent [1].
row.card: Woodbury Hill, Dorset, overlooks the Winterbourne Valley to the north and the Piddle Valley to the south. An annual fair was held here from medieval times until the mid 20th century.

row.description: Blanda (Greek: Βλάνδα), and later Blanda Julia, was an ancient city of Lucania now located at Palecastro di Tortora, Province of Cosenza, Italy [1]. In the 4th century BC the Palècastro hill was occupied by the Lucanians who rebuilt the village, fortifying it with a city wall when it took the name of Blanda [1]. A necropolis was established in the area between San Brancato and Palècastro itself [1]. The Lucanian town left a large quantity of ceramic materials [1]. The ruins of Blanda form a major archaeological site [1].
row.card: Ancient City of Blanda: in the 4th century BC Lucanians rebuilt a village on Palècastro hill and fortified it with a wall. A necropolis was established between San Brancato and Palècastro.

row.description: Huerfano Butte (English: "Orphan Butte") is a small rocky butte located on the western flank of the Santa Rita Mountains in southeastern Pima County, Arizona [1]. Huerfano Butte and the surrounding area were utilized by the Hohokam as early as circa 1100 CE [1]. Shallow bedrock forces ground water to surface in a small pool located in a wash on the south side of the butte [1]. Exposed outcrops of granite on either side of the wash have about fifty bedrock mortars, at least two small bedrock metates, and numerous smaller cupules [1]. Along the same wash is a vertical stone surface with approximately two dozen weathered pictographs painted in red hematite [1]. In 1965, Huerfano Butte gained public notoriety when a young girl discovered an extensive prehistoric jewelry cache while on a picnic with her family [1]. While exploring cracks and crevices on the butte, the young girl discovered a small pottery jar filled with about 1,500 turquoise and glycimeris shell beads and pendants [1].
row.card: On the western flank of the Santa Rita Mountains, a young girl exploring the crevices of Huerfano Butte found a small pottery jar filled with about 1,500 beads and pendants.

row.description: Metapontum or Metapontium was an ancient city of Magna Graecia, situated on the gulf of Tarentum, between the river Bradanus and the Casuentus [1]. The ruins of Metapontum are located in the frazione of Metaponto, in the comune of Bernalda, in the Province of Matera, Basilicata region, southern Italy [1]. Though Metapontum was an ancient Greek Achaean colony, various traditions assigned to it a much earlier origin [1]. At the time of the Athenian expedition to Sicily, 415 BCE, the Metapontines at first, like the other states of Magna Graecia, endeavoured to maintain a strict neutrality; but in the following year were induced to enter into an alliance with Athens [1]. It seems clear that Metapontum was at this time a flourishing and opulent city [1]. In 332 BCE, when Alexander, king of Epirus, crossed over into Italy at the invitation of the Tarentines, the Metapontines were among the first to conclude an alliance with that monarch [1]. Hence, after his defeat and death at Pandosia, 326 BCE, it was to Metapontum that his remains were sent for interment [1].
row.card: On the gulf of Tarentum lay Metapontum, a city of Magna Graecia that seems to have been flourishing and opulent. It sought strict neutrality in 415 BCE, then allied with Athens.

row.description: Stanwix is built on the site of a Roman fort known as Uxelodunum or Petriana, the former meaning "high fort" [1]. The fort was the largest on Hadrian's Wall, which adjoined the northwest edge of the fort [1]. Probably most of the Roman masonry was taken to construct other buildings [1]. However, in 2017 a bathhouse was discovered at Carlisle Cricket Club's Edenside ground [1].
row.card: Stanwix is built on Uxelodunum, the Roman high fort, largest on Hadrian's Wall. Probably most of its Roman masonry was taken to build other buildings, yet in 2017 a bathhouse came to light.

row.description: Izapa is a very large pre-Columbian era archaeological site located in the Mexican state of Chiapas; it is best known for its occupation during the Late Formative period [1]. The site is situated on the Izapa River, a tributary of the Suchiate River, near the base of Volcán Tacaná [1]. Izapa remained occupied through the Early Postclassic period, until approximately 1200 CE [1]. The New World Archaeological Foundation project at Izapa mapped 161 total mounds [1]. Izapa's Formative period core (850–100 BCE) has six major plazas [1]. The art found at the site includes sculptures of stelae and also altars that look like frogs [1]. Lowe and colleagues dated the majority of Izapa's monuments to the Guillen phase, from approximately 300 to 50 BCE, on the basis of ceramic and radiocarbon dates [1].
row.card: Near the base of Volcán Tacaná, Izapa has 161 mapped mounds. Its art includes stelae and altars that look like frogs, and most of its monuments are dated to approximately 300 to 50 BCE.

row.description: Villa Boscoreale is a name given to any of several Roman villas discovered in the district of Boscoreale, Italy [1]. They were all buried and preserved by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD, along with Pompeii and Herculaneum [1]. The only one visible in situ today is the Villa Regina, the others being reburied soon after their discovery [1]. Although these villas can be classified as "rustic" rather than of otium due to their agricultural sections and sometimes lack of the most luxurious amenities, they were often embellished with extremely luxurious decorations such as frescoes, testifying to the wealth of the owners [1]. Among the most important finds are the exquisite frescoes from the Villa of Publius Fannius Synistor and the sumptuous Boscoreale Treasure of the Villa della Pisanella, which is now displayed in several major museums [1]. In Roman times this area, like the whole of Campania, was agricultural despite its proximity to cities including Pompeii, and specialised in wine and olive oil [1].
row.card: Buried and preserved by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 AD, Villa Boscoreale gave up exquisite frescoes and a sumptuous treasure. Only the Villa Regina is still visible in situ today.

row.description: Gazma Cave is a Paleolithic dwelling site discovered between Ordubad and Sharur districts in 1983 [1]. Gazma Cave is located 3 km northeast of Tananam village, 1450 m above the sea level [1]. Archeological excavations were carried out there under the leadership of A.G.Jafarov in 1987–1990, and A.Zeynalov in 2008–2013 [1]. In addition to fauna fossils, 874 stone tools were also discovered in the cave [1]. The form of the tools is similar to those derived from Azokh and Tağlar caves [1]. 6 cultural layers were discovered in the cave [1].
row.card: Gazma Cave, a Paleolithic dwelling site 1450 m above sea level, revealed 6 cultural layers, fauna fossils and 874 stone tools, similar in form to those from Azokh and Tağlar caves.

row.description: Dykyi Sad was a fortified urban settlement of the final Bronze Age, located in the historical center of modern-day Mykolaiv, Ukraine [1]. Situated on a high promontory at the confluence of the Southern Bug and Inhul rivers, the site is an essential monument of the Belozerka culture in the Northern Black Sea region [1]. Radiocarbon and archaeological dating places its primary period of occupation between the late 13th and 10th centuries BC (predominantly 1186–925 BC) [1]. Covering an area of over 4 hectares, Dykyi Sad demonstrates a complex radial-ring architectural layout [1]. The settlement was divided into distinct structural zones: a central fortified "citadel", densely built "suburbs" [1]. This structure was protected by a system of two defensive moats [1]. To date, over 50 architectural objects have been excavated, including residential complexes with stone foundations, craft workshops, storage facilities, and unique ritual structures such as a sanctuary with a ramp [1]. The settlement was notable for its advanced bronze metallurgy, comprehensive agriculture, and bone carving [1].
row.card: On a high promontory where the Southern Bug meets the Inhul, the Dykyi Sad Archaeological Site yielded over 50 architectural objects, including craft workshops and a sanctuary with a ramp.

row.description: La Blanca is a Maya pre-Columbian Mesoamerican archaeological site in the municipality of Melchor de Mencos in the northern Petén Department of Guatemala [1]. The site is located in the lower reaches of the Mopan River valley and features a large acropolis complex [1]. La Blanca occupied a frontier zone between the northeastern and southeastern Petén regions and the site is dominated by the acropolis [1]. The end of formal occupation of the city in the Terminal Classic appears to have been violent, with evidence of a battle recovered during excavations of the acropolis [1]. Refugees appear to have occupied the city centre immediately after the collapse of formal settlement at La Blanca, but they abandoned the city for good in the 11th century, after which it was never reoccupied [1]. The site covers an area of about 26 hectares and a great many structures have been identified by archaeologists [1]. The acropolis is also distinguished by a great quantity of graffiti inscribed onto the stucco interior walls of its rooms, some of which display a considerable level of artistic skill [1].
row.card: At Sitio Arqueológico La Blanca, a Maya site, graffiti is inscribed on the acropolis's stucco walls, and its formal occupation appears to have ended violently, with evidence of a battle.

row.description: Casas Grandes (Spanish for Great Houses; also known as Paquimé) is a prehistoric archaeological site in the northern Mexican state of Chihuahua [1]. Settlement began after 1130 AD [1]. The community was abandoned approximately in 1450 AD [1]. The Casas Grandes complex is situated in a broad, fertile valley along the Casas Grandes or San Miguel River, approximately 56 kilometres south of Janos and 240 kilometres northwest of the state capital, Chihuahua [1]. Evidence indicates that Paquimé possessed an intricate water management system comprising underground drain networks, reservoirs, channels for water distribution to the residences, and a sewage system [1]. After being burned about 1340, Casas Grandes was rebuilt with multi-story apartment buildings to replace the small buildings [1].
row.card: In Chihuahua, evidence indicates Paquime had underground drains, reservoirs, water channels to its homes and a sewage system. Burned about 1340, it was rebuilt with multi-story apartments.

row.description: Teopanzolco is an Aztec archaeological site in the Mexican state of Morelos [1]. Most of the visible remains date from the Middle to Late Postclassic Period [1]. Teopanzolco was built upon a hill formed from a lava flow [1]. The prehispanic history of Teopanzolco was brought to a close by the Spanish Conquest in 1521 [1]. Only the ceremonial centre of Teopanzolco has been preserved [1]. Although the site had been developed by both the Tlahuicas and the Aztecs, the dominant architectural style and the majority of the excavated ceramics are Aztec in origin [1].
row.card: Built on a hill formed from a lava flow, Zona Arqueológica Teopanzolco has only its ceremonial centre preserved. The Spanish Conquest in 1521 closed its prehispanic history.
